response.text:
## (1) Boxplots and interpretation of the given ANOVA p-value

First sort each sample:

- RU: \(31,56,78,143,210\)
- PS: \(26,30,37,54,70\)
- UC: \(21,22,24,36,65\)

Using the usual Tukey/R boxplot hinges for \(n=5\), the five-number summaries are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc|c}
\text{School} & \min & Q_1 & \text{Median} & Q_3 & \max & \text{IQR}\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 31 & 56 & 78 & 143 & 210 & 87\\
\text{PS} & 26 & 30 & 37 & 54 & 70 & 24\\
\text{UC} & 21 & 22 & 24 & 36 & 65 & 14
\end{array}
\]

So the boxplots would show:

- RU has the largest median and by far the largest spread.
- PS and UC are much closer to each other, with substantial overlap.
- All three groups have long upper tails relative to their lower tails, especially UC because of the observation 65.

The given ANOVA p-value is approximately \(0.06\). Thus the classical one-way ANOVA gives marginal evidence against equality of the three school means: not significant at the \(5\%\) level, but significant at the \(10\%\) level. Visually, this is consistent with the boxplots: RU appears higher, but the RU sample also has very large variability, and the samples are tiny.

The one-way ANOVA \(F\)-test assumes independent observations and approximately normal errors with common variance:

\[
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ij}\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2).
\]

The boxplots suggest these assumptions are questionable:

- The samples are right-skewed.
- The group spreads are very unequal: RU is much more variable than PS and UC.
- With only \(n=5\) per group, normality is hard to justify.

So the original ANOVA p-value should be interpreted cautiously.

---

## (2) Spread-vs-level plot and optimal power transformation

For a spread-vs-level plot, use the group median as the level and the IQR as the spread.

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\text{School} & \text{Median} & \text{IQR}\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 78 & 87\\
\text{PS} & 37 & 24\\
\text{UC} & 24 & 14
\end{array}
\]

Plot

\[
\log(\text{IQR}) \quad \text{versus} \quad \log(\text{Median}).
\]

The three log-points are approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\text{School} & \log(\text{Median}) & \log(\text{IQR})\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 4.357 & 4.466\\
\text{PS} & 3.611 & 3.178\\
\text{UC} & 3.178 & 2.639
\end{array}
\]

Fitting a line

\[
\log(\text{IQR}) = a + b\log(\text{Median})
\]

gives approximately

\[
b \approx 1.57.
\]

By the Tukey spread-vs-level rule, the variance-stabilizing power is

\[
\lambda = 1-b \approx 1-1.57 = -0.57.
\]

Thus the optimal power transformation is approximately

\[
y \mapsto y^{-0.57}.
\]

A convenient nearby ladder-of-powers choice is

\[
y \mapsto y^{-1/2},
\]

or, to preserve the order of the original observations,

\[
y \mapsto 2\left(1-y^{-1/2}\right),
\]

which is an affine transformation of \(y^{-1/2}\) and therefore gives the same ANOVA \(F\)-statistic.

---

## (3) ANOVA after transformation

Using the estimated transformation \(z=y^{-0.57}\), the transformed group means are approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{School} & \bar z_i\\
\hline
\text{RU} & 0.0864\\
\text{PS} & 0.1239\\
\text{UC} & 0.1468
\end{array}
\]

The one-way ANOVA table on the transformed scale is approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\text{Source} & df & SS & MS & F\\
\hline
\text{School} & 2 & 0.00928 & 0.00464 & 4.09\\
\text{Error} & 12 & 0.01361 & 0.00113 & \\
\hline
\text{Total} & 14 & 0.02289 & &
\end{array}
\]

Thus

\[
F \approx 4.09, \qquad df=(2,12).
\]

For \(F_{2,12}\),

\[
p \approx 0.044.
\]

So after the variance-stabilizing transformation, the school effect is significant at the \(5\%\) level. The evidence of differences among schools is driven mainly by RU being higher than PS and UC, while PS and UC remain relatively close.
